claims.source: The hemiellipsoid body is well defined, with a voluminous, hemispherical cap region (HNcap) located dorsally (Figures 3, 4, 5D and 6A–F) and displaying synapsin-like immunoreactivity (SYNir) (Figure 6G–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The cap region of the hemiellipsoid body displays synapsin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: The hemiellipsoid body is well defined, with a voluminous, hemispherical cap region (HNcap) located dorsally (Figures 3, 4, 5D and 6A–F) and displaying synapsin-like immunoreactivity (SYNir) (Figure 6G–I).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The core region of the hemiellipsoid body is fused posteriorly with the terminal medulla in R. exoculata.
claims.source: The core region of the hemiellipsoid body (HNcore) is fused posteriorly with the terminal medulla (Figures 4F and 6B,D,E).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The cap and core regions of the hemiellipsoid body are separated by an arcuate intermediate layer.
claims.source: The cap and core regions are separated by an arcuate intermediate layer (IL) (Figures 4E and 6A,B,D,E,G–I)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The intermediate layer receives parallel afferent fibers from the terminal medulla anteriorly.
claims.source: The cap and core regions are separated by an arcuate intermediate layer (IL) (Figures 4E and 6A,B,D,E,G–I) which receives parallel afferent fibers from the terminal medulla anteriorly (namely the HN-TM tract) (Figures 3A,B, 4F and 6A–C, black asterisks)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The intermediate layer receives a massive bundle of neurites from somata in the cell cluster (5) at the medial side.
claims.source: The cap and core regions are separated by an arcuate intermediate layer (IL) (Figures 4E and 6A,B,D,E,G–I) which receives parallel afferent fibers from the terminal medulla anteriorly (namely the HN-TM tract) (Figures 3A,B, 4F and 6A–C, black asterisks) and a massive bundle of neurites from somata in the cell cluster (5) at the medial side (Figures 4E, 5D and 6C–E, white asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Some of the intermediate layer fibers display allatostatin-like immunoreactivity near the cap region.
claims.source: Some of the intermediate layer fibers display allatostatin-like immunoreactivity (ASTir) near the cap region (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6G showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The intermediate layer is devoid of synapsin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: The intermediate layer is devoid of SYNir (Figure 6J).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6J showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The cap region of the hemiellipsoid body is characterized by synaptic sites forming microglomeruli.
claims.source: The cap region is characterized by synaptic sites forming microglomeruli (Figure 6H')
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6H' showing data.

claims.claim: The cap region is innervated by serotonergic neurons.
claims.source: The cap region is characterized by synaptic sites forming microglomeruli (Figure 6H') and is also innervated by serotonergic neurons (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6H showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The cell cluster (5) contains approximately 30,000 cell somata of the so-called globuli cells.
claims.source: The cell cluster (5) is voluminous (Figures 3C, 4B and 6B–E,I,J) and contains approximately 30,000 cell somata of the so-called globuli cells (Wolff et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements and refers to a citation.

claims.claim: The hemiellipsoid body receives input from the olfactory neuropils via the projection neuron tract in the posterior region.
claims.source: The hemiellipsoid body receives input from the olfactory neuropils via the projection neuron tract (PNT) in the posterior region (Figures 3A and 6B,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla is a large and complex neuropil.
claims.source: The terminal medulla is a large and complex neuropil.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: Anteriorly, the terminal medulla is shaped like a sphere.
claims.source: Anteriorly, it is shaped like a sphere (Figures 3, 4A,C,F and 6A–C)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla connects to the intermediate layer of the hemiellipsoid body via the HN-TM tract.
claims.source: Anteriorly, it is shaped like a sphere (Figures 3, 4A,C,F and 6A–C), and it connects to the intermediate layer of the hemiellipsoid body via the HN-TM tract (Figures 3A,D, 4F and 6A–C, black asterisks).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Posterior to the anterior region, the terminal medulla is large, crossed by seemingly unstructured networks of fibers.
claims.source: Posterior to this region, the terminal medulla is large, crossed by seemingly unstructured networks of fibers (Figures 3A, 4C,F and 6D–F) and displays SYNir (Figure 6I,J).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla displays synapsin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: Posterior to this region, the terminal medulla is large, crossed by seemingly unstructured networks of fibers (Figures 3A, 4C,F and 6D–F) and displays SYNir (Figure 6I,J).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla is innervated by neurites from the cell cluster (4).
claims.source: It is innervated by neurites from the cell cluster (4) (Figure 6D, white arrowhead)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6D showing data.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla connects to the intermediate layer of the hemiellipsoid body via radiating fiber bundles.
claims.source: It is innervated by neurites from the cell cluster (4) (Figure 6D, white arrowhead), and further connects again to the intermediate layer of the hemiellipsoid body via radiating fiber bundles (Figure 6E, black arrowheads).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6E showing data.

claims.claim: The median protocerebrum comprises two medially fused neuropils, the anterior and posterior medial protocerebral neuropils.
claims.source: The median protocerebrum (mPC) comprises two medially fused neuropils, the anterior (AMPN) and posterior (PMPN) medial protocerebral neuropils.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The AMPN connects to the terminal medulla of the lateral protocerebrum anteriorly via the protocerebral tract.
claims.source: The AMPN connects to the terminal medulla of the lateral protocerebrum anteriorly via the protocerebral tract (PT) (Figures 3B and 6C,D)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The PMPN connects to the terminal medulla via the posterior protocerebral tract, which contains neurites with strong serotonin-immunoreactivity.
claims.source: The AMPN connects to the terminal medulla of the lateral protocerebrum anteriorly via the protocerebral tract (PT) (Figures 3B and 6C,D) and the PMPN via the posterior protocerebral tract (PPT), the latter containing neurites with strong serotonin-immunoreactivity (5HTir) (Figure 7C)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The AMPN and PMPN are separated by the unpaired central body neuropil.
claims.source: Both, the AMPN and PMPN are separated by the unpaired central body neuropil (CB) (Figure 3)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 3 showing data.

claims.claim: The central body displays allatostatin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: Both, the AMPN and PMPN are separated by the unpaired central body neuropil (CB) (Figure 3), which displays ASTir (Figure 7B)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 7B showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The central body displays weak synapsin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: Both, the AMPN and PMPN are separated by the unpaired central body neuropil (CB) (Figure 3), which displays ASTir (Figure 7B), weak SYNir (Figure 7A)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 7A showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The central body displays strong serotonin-immunoreactivity.
claims.source: Both, the AMPN and PMPN are separated by the unpaired central body neuropil (CB) (Figure 3), which displays ASTir (Figure 7B), weak SYNir (Figure 7A) and strong 5HTir (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 7C showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The median protocerebrum contains many fibers from serotonergic neurons.
claims.source: Overall, the median protocerebrum contains many fibers from serotonergic neurons, partly from the cell cluster (x) (which likely refers to the cell clusters (12 , 13) and (17) according to Sandeman et al., 1992)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Posteriorly to the central body, fiber bundles of the projection neuron tracts from both hemispheres meet in a region with strong synapsin-like immunoreactivity, called the projection neuron tract central neuropil.
claims.source: Posteriorly to the central body, fiber bundles of the projection neuron tracts from both hemispheres meet in a region with strong SYNir, that we will call the projection neuron tract central neuropil (PNTCN) (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 7A showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: In the deutocerebrum, a paired neuropil with a conspicuous structure is located laterally, the lobe-shaped olfactory neuropil.
claims.source: In the deutocerebrum, a paired neuropil with a conspicuous structure is located laterally, the lobe-shaped olfactory neuropil (ON) (Figures 3, 4A–D,F, 5D and 8A–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropil is composed of approximately 180 wedge-shaped neuropil units, the olfactory glomeruli, which are arranged radially around the periphery of a non-synaptic core.
claims.source: It is composed of approximately 180 wedge-shaped neuropil units, the olfactory glomeruli (og), which are arranged radially around the periphery of a non-synaptic core (Figures 3B, 4F, 5D and 8A–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Each olfactory glomerulus shows strong synapsin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: Each glomerulus shows strong SYNir (Figure 8E–F)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: Allatostatin-like immunoreactivity highlights a subdivision of each olfactory glomerulus into a cap, subcap and base region.
claims.source: Each glomerulus shows strong SYNir (Figure 8E–F), as well as ASTir which highlights a subdivision of each glomerulus into a cap (c), subcap (sbc) and base (b) region (Figure 8E').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 8E' showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The sensory input of the olfactory neuropil comes from the olfactory sensory neurons innervating the aesthetasc sensilla on the lateral flagellum of the antenna 1.
claims.source: The sensory input of the olfactory neuropil comes from the olfactory sensory neurons innervating the aesthetasc sensilla on the lateral flagellum of the antenna 1.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on established knowledge of crustacean neuroanatomy.

claims.claim: The somata of olfactory interneurons located in the cell cluster (9/11) innervate fibers of the olfactory neuropil, some of which display allatostatin-like immunoreactivity.
claims.source: The somata of olfactory interneurons located in the cell cluster (9/11) innervate fibers of the olfactory neuropil, some of which display ASTir (Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 8H showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: Olfactory interneuron fibers enter via the medial foramen into the core of the olfactory neuropil.
claims.source: These fibers enter via the medial foramen (mF) into the core of the neuropil (Figure 8C,E)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: From the core, olfactory interneuron fibers target the glomerular base region or cross to the lateral foramen to spread out laterally and innervate the glomerular cap region.
claims.source: These fibers enter via the medial foramen (mF) into the core of the neuropil (Figure 8C,E), from where they target the glomerular base region (Figure 8E), or cross to the lateral foramen (lF) (Figure 8A,C,E) to spread out laterally and innervate the glomerular cap region (Figure 8E, white arrowhead).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The medial foramen is the place where efferent fibers exit from the olfactory neuropil.
claims.source: The medial foramen is also the place where efferent fibers exit from the olfactory neuropil.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The efferent fibers exiting from the olfactory neuropil are the axons of the olfactory projection neurons that form the projection neuron tract.
claims.source: These are the axons of the olfactory projection neurons that form the projection neuron tract (Figure 8B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: A projection neuron tract neuropil is identifiable close to the ascending branch of the projection neuron tract.
claims.source: A projection neuron tract neuropil (PNTN) as known from other decapods (e.g. Sandeman et al., 1992; Harzsch and Hansson, 2008; Krieger et al., 2012a) is identifiable close to the ascending branch of the tract (Figure 8E,F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations and figures.

claims.claim: The projection neuron tract transverses the median protocerebrum and projects to the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.source: The projection neuron tract then transverses the median protocerebrum and projects to the lateral protocerebrum (see above).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The lateral antenna one neuropil is located medially to the olfactory neuropil.
claims.source: The lateral antenna one neuropil (LAN) is located medially to the olfactory neuropil.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The lateral antenna one neuropil is U-shaped.
claims.source: It is U-shaped (Figures 3 and 8A,B,H)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The lateral antenna one neuropil displays strong synapsin-like immunoreactivity and allatostatin-like immunoreactivity, which reveals a transversely stratified pattern.
claims.source: It is U-shaped (Figures 3 and 8A,B,H) and displays strong SYNir, as well as ASTir, which reveals a transversely stratified pattern (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 8G showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The lateral antenna one neuropil connects posterodorsally to the median protocerebrum.
claims.source: This neuropil connects posterodorsally to the median protocerebrum (Figure 8G,H).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The median antenna one neuropil is small, poorly defined, and located in the center of the deutocerebrum, below the anterior region of the median protocerebrum and between the paired lateral antenna one neuropils.
claims.source: The median antenna one neuropil (MAN) is small, poorly defined, and located in the center of the deutocerebrum, below the anterior region of the median protocerebrum and between the paired lateral antenna one neuropils (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 3 showing data.

claims.claim: The tritocerebrum comprises the antenna two neuropil, which has a cylindrical shape and lies in front of the oesophageal connectives.
claims.source: The tritocerebrum comprises the antenna two neuropil (AnN), which has a cylindrical shape and lies in front of the oesophageal connectives (Figures 3 and 4, 8 HA).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Synapsin-like immunoreactivity and allatostatin-like immunoreactivity show a transversely stratified pattern within the antenna two neuropil.
claims.source: SYNir and ASTir show a transversely stratified pattern within this neuropil (Figure 8I).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 8I showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: The tegumentary neuropil is located posterodorsally, poorly differentiated from the antenna two neuropil.
claims.source: Poorly differentiated from the antenna two neuropil, the tegumentary neuropil (TN) is located posterodorsally (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 3 showing data.

claims.claim: The organ of Bellonci is typical for many crustaceans but its sensory function remains unclear.
claims.source: The organ of Bellonci (OB) is typical for many crustaceans but its sensory function remains unclear (Chaigneau, 1994).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In R. exoculata, the organ of Bellonci is conspicuous and comprises onion bodies structures connected to a well-developed nerve tract.
claims.source: In R. exoculata, this organ is conspicuous and comprises onion bodies (Ob) structures connected to a well-developed nerve tract (OBNv).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The onion bodies are situated on the anterolateral side of the brain, in front of the hemiellipsoid body.
claims.source: The onion bodies are situated on the anterolateral side of the brain, in front of the hemiellipsoid body (Figures 3, 4A–D, 5D and 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The onion bodies represent a cluster of about fifty densely packed lobules.
claims.source: They represent a cluster of about fifty densely packed lobules (Figure 9A,B)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Many lobules of the onion bodies contain elements of granular appearance.
claims.source: They represent a cluster of about fifty densely packed lobules (Figure 9A,B), many of them containing elements of granular appearance (Figure 9B', white arrowhead).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 9B' showing data.

claims.claim: Some lobules are located in the proximal region of the organ of Bellonci nerve.
claims.source: Some lobules are further located in the proximal region of OBNv (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 9B showing data.

claims.claim: The organ of Bellonci nerve is large in its proximal region, and progressively tapers as it draws away from the brain.
claims.source: This nerve is large in its proximal region, and progressively tapers as it draws away from the brain (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 9A showing data.

claims.claim: Anterodorsally, the organ of Bellonci nerve extends through the retinal layers and connects underneath the cuticle of the ocular plate.
claims.source: Anterodorsally, the nerve extends through the retinal layers and connects underneath the cuticle of the ocular plate (Figure 9C,C').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 9C,C' showing data.

claims.claim: The myoarterial formation underlies the dorsal carapace and is located between the paired eyes, above the brain.
claims.source: The myoarterial formation (maf) (or cor frontale, auxiliary heart) underlies the dorsal carapace and is located between the paired eyes, above the brain (Figure 10A,B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The myoarterial formation is voluminous, being almost as long as the elongated retina.
claims.source: This organ is voluminous, being almost as long as the elongated retina, and extends ventrally towards the dorsal region of the brain (Figure 10B',C').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Two adjacent and parallel muscle bundles penetrate through the myoarterial formation.
claims.source: Two adjacent and parallel muscle bundles (mafm) penetrate through the myoarterial formation (Figure 10A)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 10A showing data.

claims.claim: The muscle bundles attach to the cuticle via tendons located either anteriorly or dorsally.
claims.source: Two adjacent and parallel muscle bundles (mafm) penetrate through the myoarterial formation (Figure 10A) and attach to the cuticle via tendons located either anteriorly (Ta) or dorsally (Td) (Figure 10B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Two thinner muscular bundles cross the myoarterial formation in its middle region, perpendicular to the main adjacent muscles.
claims.source: Two thinner muscular bundles cross the myoarterial formation in its middle region, perpendicular to the main adjacent muscles, and are attached both to the dorsal and ventral cuticle of the cephalothorax, by secondary dorsal and ventral tendons (T'd, Figure 10B,C; T'v, Figure 10B').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Anteriorly, below the junction of the ocular plate with the dorsal carapace, the myoarterial formation gives rise to three conspicuous, large cerebral arteries, a central cerebral artery and two ophthalmic arteries.
claims.source: Anteriorly, below the junction of the ocular plate with the dorsal carapace, the myoarterial formation gives rise to three conspicuous, large cerebral arteries, a central cerebral artery (CA) and two ophthalmic arteries (OA), which all make a steep U-turn and extend parallel towards the dorsal side of the brain (Figure 10B,C, arrowhead).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The central cerebral artery divides into three smaller arteries, one median and two lateral ones.
claims.source: In an anterodorsal position, median to the hemiellipsoid bodies, the central cerebral artery divides into three smaller arteries, one median (CAM) and two lateral ones (CAL) (Figure 10B',C').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The median artery passes over the brain, between the two spherical masses of the lateral protocerebrum, and then divides into two branches.
claims.source: The median artery passes over the brain, between the two spherical masses of the lateral protocerebrum, and then divides into two branches, one entering the brain posteriorly, at the level of the median protocerebrum, and a larger one merging with the ventral region of the myoarterial formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: Part of the hemolymph in the cerebral artery goes back into the myoarterial system, suggesting a loop system.
claims.source: This suggests a loop system wherein part of the hemolymph in the cerebral artery goes back into the myoarterial system.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference from the anatomical observations.

claims.claim: The lateral cerebral arteries are coil-shaped and enter the brain above the insertion of the antenna one nerve to target the olfactory neuropils and the lateral antenna one neuropils in the deutocerebrum.
claims.source: The lateral cerebral arteries are coil-shaped and enter the brain above the insertion of the antenna one nerve to target for instance the olfactory neuropils and the lateral antenna one neuropils in the deutocerebrum.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The ophthalmic arteries enter the brain in a posterodorsal position and target the visual neuropils and the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.source: The ophthalmic arteries enter the brain in a posterodorsal position (Figure 10C') and target the visual neuropils and the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 10C' showing data.

claims.claim: The cerebral vascular system of R. exoculata is considerably developed, with blood vessels supplying all brain neuropils and cell clusters.
claims.source: The cerebral vascular system of R. exoculata is considerably developed, with blood vessels supplying all brain neuropils and cell clusters, as in other crustaceans, including large vessels that irrigate the visual neuropils (Figure 5A,C), the deutocerebrum (Figure 8B) and the lateral protocerebrum (Figure 9B,B').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The number of olfactory glomeruli and their unitary volume in R. exoculata fit within the ranges displayed by other decapods.
claims.source: The number of olfactory glomeruli and their unitary volume in R. exoculata fit within the ranges displayed by other decapods.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on comparative data in Table 1.

claims.claim: R. exoculata presents relatively small olfactory neuropils compared to other species with roughly the same body size, such as Palaemon elegans and Coenobita clypeatus.
claims.source: However, this species presents relatively small olfactory neuropils (excluding the fibrous core) compared to other species with roughly the same body size, such as the caridean Palaemon elegans and the anomuran Coenobita clypeatus.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on comparative data in Table 1.

claims.claim: Other species of about the same body size as R. exoculata (e.g. Procambarus clarkii and Saduria entomon) possess olfactory neuropils of even smaller volume than those of R. exoculata.
claims.source: Yet, other species of about the same body size (e.g. the crayfish Procambarus clarkii and the isopod Saduria entomon) possess olfactory neuropils of even smaller volume than those of R. exoculata.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on comparative data in Table 1.

claims.claim: The higher integrative centers are especially well-developed in R. exoculata in relation to the relative size of the olfactory neuropils, compared to other crustaceans.
claims.source: The higher integrative centers (i.e. the hemiellipsoid body and the terminal medulla, associated with cell cluster 5) are especially well-developed in R. exoculata in relation to the relative size of the olfactory neuropils, compared to other crustaceans (Figure 11).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 11 showing comparative data.

claims.claim: The higher integrative centers in R. exoculata occupy approximately 25% of the total brain volume.
claims.source: As an example, from relative volumes obtained from 3D reconstructions, the higher integrative centers in R. exoculata occupy approximately 25% of the total brain volume
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The higher integrative centers in Palaemon elegans occupy approximately 22% of the total brain volume.
claims.source: As an example, from relative volumes obtained from 3D reconstructions, the higher integrative centers in R. exoculata occupy approximately 25% of the total brain volume, similarly to the caridean shrimp P. elegans (22%)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The higher integrative centers in Birgus latro occupy approximately 13% of the total brain volume.
claims.source: As an example, from relative volumes obtained from 3D reconstructions, the higher integrative centers in R. exoculata occupy approximately 25% of the total brain volume, similarly to the caridean shrimp P. elegans (22%) but twice more than in the giant robber crab Birgus latro (13%).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils of P. elegans occupy roughly two times more volume than those of R. exoculata.
claims.source: However, the olfactory neuropils of P. elegans and B. latro occupy roughly two and six times more volume than those of R. exoculata
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils of B. latro occupy roughly six times more volume than those of R. exoculata.
claims.source: However, the olfactory neuropils of P. elegans and B. latro occupy roughly two and six times more volume than those of R. exoculata
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils represent 2.7% of the total brain volume in R. exoculata.
claims.source: However, the olfactory neuropils of P. elegans and B. latro occupy roughly two and six times more volume than those of R. exoculata, values that represent 4.2%, 17% and 2.7% of the total brain volume, respectively in these species.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils represent 4.2% of the total brain volume in P. elegans.
claims.source: However, the olfactory neuropils of P. elegans and B. latro occupy roughly two and six times more volume than those of R. exoculata, values that represent 4.2%, 17% and 2.7% of the total brain volume, respectively in these species.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils represent 17% of the total brain volume in B. latro.
claims.source: However, the olfactory neuropils of P. elegans and B. latro occupy roughly two and six times more volume than those of R. exoculata, values that represent 4.2%, 17% and 2.7% of the total brain volume, respectively in these species.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on measurements from 3D reconstructions.

claims.claim: The general anatomy of the brain of R. exoculata corresponds in many aspects to the ground pattern of the malacostracan crustacean brain.
claims.source: The general anatomy of the brain of R. exoculata corresponds in many aspects to the ground pattern of the malacostracan crustacean brain (Kenning et al., 2013), including the subdivision into proto-, deuto- and tritocerebrum, the location of main nerves and the presence of distinct cell clusters.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The brain of R. exoculata exhibits morphological differences to other malacostracans, especially at the level of the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.source: However, the brain of R. exoculata also exhibits morphological differences to other malacostracans, especially at the level of the lateral protocerebrum.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The organ of Bellonci is especially conspicuous in R. exoculata.
claims.source: The organ of Bellonci is especially conspicuous (also observed by Charmantier-Daures and Segonzac, 1998), but its sensory function remains elusive.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: In crustaceans, the neurovascular system has been described mainly in crayfish, crabs, and spiny lobsters.
claims.source: In crustaceans, the neurovascular system has been described mainly in crayfish (Chaves da Silva et al., 2013; Scholz et al., 2018), crabs (McGaw, 2005; McGaw and Reiber, 2002; Sandeman, 1967) and spiny lobsters (Steinacker, 1979) (reviews in McMahon, 2001; Steinacker, 1979; Steinacker, 1978; Wilkens, 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The brain and eyes are supplied with hemolymph via the anterior aorta system, which originates antero-medially from the heart and runs between the stomach and the dorsal integument.
claims.source: The brain and eyes are supplied with hemolymph via the anterior aorta system, which originates antero-medially from the heart and runs between the stomach and the dorsal integument (Scholz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A dilatation of the anterior aorta, the myoarterial formation, functions as an auxiliary heart and pumps the hemolymph specifically towards the anterior part of the central nervous system.
claims.source: Anteriorly, a dilatation of the anterior aorta, the myoarterial formation (Scholz et al., 2018; also named the cor frontale in for example McGaw (2005); Steinacker (1978) which functions as an auxiliary heart, pumps the hemolymph specifically towards the anterior part of the central nervous system.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In malacostracan crustaceans, the myoarterial formation above the brain gives rise to a descending cerebral artery, which supplies the median brain, and to two ophthalmic arteries that turn laterally and extend into the eyestalks to supply the visual neuropils.
claims.source: In malacostracan crustaceans, the myoarterial formation above the brain gives rise to a descending cerebral artery, which supplies the median brain, and to two ophthalmic arteries that turn laterally and extend into the eyestalks to supply the visual neuropils (Chaves da Silva et al., 2013; McGaw, 2005; Scholz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In R. exoculata, consistent with the absence of eyestalks, the myoarterial formation and its arteries differ in shape, size and position from those previously described in other malacostracans.
claims.source: In R. exoculata, consistent with the absence of eyestalks, the myoarterial formation and its arteries differ in shape, size and position from those previously described in other malacostracans (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 10 showing data.

claims.claim: In crustaceans, the perfusion of the brain is modulated by physiological or environmental factors, such as hypoxia.
claims.source: In crustaceans, the perfusion of the brain is modulated by physiological or environmental factors, such as hypoxia (Reiber and McMahon, 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The mixing of the hydrothermal fluid with the surrounding seawater can create hypoxic conditions for vent animals.
claims.source: Because the pure hydrothermal fluid is anoxic, the mixing of the fluid with the surrounding seawater can create hypoxic conditions for vent animals (Childress and Fisher, 1992; Schmidt et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Known adaptations to hypoxia in vent crustaceans include an hemocyanin with a higher affinity for oxygen compared to shallow-water species.
claims.source: Known adaptations to hypoxia in vent crustaceans include an hemocyanin with a higher affinity for oxygen compared to shallow-water species (Chausson et al., 2004; Lallier and Truchot, 1997; Sanders et al., 1988).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: A very pronounced capillary network was observed in hydrothermal vent alvinellid polychaetes.
claims.source: A very pronounced capillary network was also observed in hydrothermal vent alvinellid polychaetes (Hourdez and Lallier, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The pronounced myoarterial formation and large cerebral arteries in R. exoculata could represent a particularly efficient system for oxygen delivery to the brain to cope with low availability of oxygen.
claims.source: Accordingly, the pronounced myoarterial formation and large cerebral arteries in R. exoculata could represent a particularly efficient system for oxygen delivery to the brain to cope with low availability of oxygen.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation based on the anatomical observations.

claims.claim: Van Dover et al. (1989) described the R. exoculata eyes as a pair of large anteriorly fused organs that underlie the transparent dorsal carapace of the cephalothorax.
claims.source: Van Dover et al. (1989) described the R. exoculata eyes as a pair of large anteriorly fused organs that underlie the transparent dorsal carapace of the cephalothorax and demonstrated the presence of rhodopsin-like visual pigments in high quantity, with a maximum absorption at 500 nm.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Van Dover et al. (1989) demonstrated the presence of rhodopsin-like visual pigments in high quantity in R. exoculata eyes, with a maximum absorption at 500 nm.
claims.source: Van Dover et al. (1989) described the R. exoculata eyes as a pair of large anteriorly fused organs that underlie the transparent dorsal carapace of the cephalothorax and demonstrated the presence of rhodopsin-like visual pigments in high quantity, with a maximum absorption at 500 nm.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Subsequent analyses showed that the eyes of R. exoculata comprise a smooth cornea located above a dense layer of hypertrophied rhabdoms, under which a white layer of reflective cells, the tapetum, is located and maximizes the absorption of light by the photoreceptors.
claims.source: Subsequent analyses showed that the eyes comprise a smooth cornea located above a dense layer of hypertrophied rhabdoms, under which a white layer of reflective cells, the tapetum, is located and maximizes the absorption of light by the photoreceptors (Chamberlain, 2000; Jinks et al., 1998; Nuckley et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The rhabdoms of R. exoculata were strongly degenerated, a process ascribed to the damaging exposure to intense light during sampling.
claims.source: The eyes of R. exoculata lack the dioptric apparatus which characterizes the ommatidia of compounds eye of pelagic and shallow water crustaceans and thus cannot form images (Chamberlain, 2000; Jinks et al., 1998; Nuckley et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1995), but their highly sensitive naked retina seems adapted for the detection of low ambient light levels, to the detriment of spatial resolution (Chamberlain, 2000; Van Dover et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The eyes of R. exoculata lack the dioptric apparatus which characterizes the ommatidia of compounds eye of pelagic and shallow water crustaceans and thus cannot form images.
claims.source: The eyes of R. exoculata lack the dioptric apparatus which characterizes the ommatidia of compounds eye of pelagic and shallow water crustaceans and thus cannot form images (Chamberlain, 2000; Jinks et al., 1998; Nuckley et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1995)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The highly sensitive naked retina of R. exoculata seems adapted for the detection of low ambient light levels, to the detriment of spatial resolution.
claims.source: The eyes of R. exoculata lack the dioptric apparatus which characterizes the ommatidia of compounds eye of pelagic and shallow water crustaceans and thus cannot form images (Chamberlain, 2000; Jinks et al., 1998; Nuckley et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1995), but their highly sensitive naked retina seems adapted for the detection of low ambient light levels, to the detriment of spatial resolution (Chamberlain, 2000; Van Dover et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: In malacostracan crustaceans, the visual input from the compound eyes is processed by a suite of retinotopic visual neuropils, usually but not exclusively located within the moveable eyestalks.
claims.source: In malacostracan crustaceans, the visual input from the compound eyes is processed by a suite of retinotopic visual neuropils, usually but not exclusively located within the moveable eyestalks (Figure 2B) (Strausfeld, 2012; Loesel et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The absence of eyestalks of R. exoculata coincides with a strong size reduction and fusion of the visual neuropils with the median brain.
claims.source: The absence of eyestalks of R. exoculata coincides with a strong size reduction and fusion of the visual neuropils with the median brain (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 2A showing data.

claims.claim: Charmantier-Daures and Segonzac (1998) and Gaten et al. (1998) differentiated three visual neuropils in R. exoculata, namely the lamina, medulla, and lobula.
claims.source: Nevertheless, already Charmantier-Daures and Segonzac (1998) and Gaten et al. (1998) differentiated three visual neuropils in R. exoculata, namely the lamina, medulla, and lobula, as in the ground pattern of the Malacostraca.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The dorsal expansion of the flattened lamina, that extends in parallel to the retina, may indicate a retinotopic projection of photoreceptor input onto the lamina which could allow the animals to extract directional information from light sources above.
claims.source: The dorsal expansion of the flattened lamina, that extends in parallel to the retina, may indicate a retinotopic projection of photoreceptor input onto the lamina which could allow the animals to extract directional information from light sources above but this issue must be addressed in future experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation.

claims.claim: In the medulla, immunohistochemistry revealed an outer layer, suggesting a subdivision of the medulla into an outer and inner region, as seen in crayfish.
claims.source: In the medulla, immunohistochemistry revealed an outer layer (Figure 6I) (which is also faintly visible in histological sections, Figure 5B,C), suggesting a subdivision of the medulla into an outer and inner region, as seen in crayfish (Strausfeld and Nassel, 1981).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation and figures showing data.

claims.claim: No stratification was observed for the lobula.
claims.source: No such stratification was observed for the lobula (Figure 5A,B)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: Synapsin immunoreactivity was weak in the lobula.
claims.source: No such stratification was observed for the lobula (Figure 5A,B), and synapsin immunoreactivity was weak in this most proximal neuropil (Figure 6J)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 6J showing immunohistochemistry data.

claims.claim: In malacostracans with well-developed compound eyes, the lobula displays numerous, neurochemically diverse strata.
claims.source: No such stratification was observed for the lobula (Figure 5A,B), and synapsin immunoreactivity was weak in this most proximal neuropil (Figure 6J), although in malacostracans with well-developed compound eyes, the lobula displays numerous, neurochemically diverse strata (e.g. Brachyura and Anomura, Harzsch and Hansson, 2008; Krieger et al., 2012b; Krieger et al., 2010; Wolff et al., 2012; Polanska et al., 2007; Meth et al., 2017; Strausfeld, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The simplified structure of the lobula, which in other malacostracans plays a role in motion detection, might mirror the inability of the eye to form images.
claims.source: The simplified structure of the lobula, which in other malacostracans plays a role in motion detection (Strausfeld, 2012), might mirror the inability of the eye to form images.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The lobula plate, a fourth visual neuropil present in several malacostracan taxa, could not be identified in R. exoculata.
claims.source: Also, the lobula plate, a fourth visual neuropil present in several malacostracan taxa (e.g. Bengochea et al., 2018; Harzsch and Hansson, 2008; Krieger et al., 2012a; Krieger et al., 2010; Sztarker et al., 2009; Meth et al., 2017; Strausfeld, 2005; Kenning et al., 2013; Kenning and Harzsch, 2013; Sinakevitch et al., 2003) could not be identified in R. exoculata.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The lobula plate has been suggested to mediate optokinetic control, necessary to track moving objects.
claims.source: The lobula plate has been suggested to mediate optokinetic control, necessary to track moving objects (e.g. conspecifics, preys, predators) (Sztarker et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The loss of the lobula plate in R. exoculata is consistent with the lack of image formation, necessary for tracking moving objects.
claims.source: Such a role is consistent with the loss of the lobula plate in R. exoculata, which lacks the realization of image formation, necessary for tracking moving objects.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference.

claims.claim: Many eyeless representatives of Crustacea have partially or totally lost their central visual pathways while adapting to a life under dim-light conditions or complete darkness.
claims.source: Many eyeless representatives of Crustacea have partially or totally lost their central visual pathways while adapting to a life under dim-light conditions or complete darkness (e.g. Ramm and Scholtz, 2017; Stegner et al., 2015; Elofsson and Hessler, 1990; Stegner and Richter, 2011; Fanenbruck et al., 2004; Brenneis and Richter, 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: It is likely that the reduction of visual nervous tissues is promoted under the selective pressure of dim-light or darkness conditions resulting in less energy expenditure for organisms living in constant or partial darkness.
claims.source: It is likely that the reduction of these nervous tissues is promoted under the selective pressure of those conditions resulting in a less energy expenditure for organisms living in constant or partial darkness, since eliminating neuronal structures which are no longer useful saves considerable amounts of energy (Klaus et al., 2013; Moran et al., 2015; Niven and Laughlin, 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The fact that neuronal elements indicative for a functional visual system are present in R. exoculata must mean that there is light to exploit as an environmental cue.
claims.source: However, the fact that neuronal elements indicative for a functional visual system are present in R. exoculata must mean that there is light to exploit as an environmental cue.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference.

claims.claim: The unusual nature of the visual system of R. exoculata suggests that it exploits a specific type of signal.
claims.source: Also, the unusual nature of the visual system of R. exoculata suggests that it exploits a specific type of signal.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference.

claims.claim: One prominent hypothesis refers to the thermal black body radiation emitted by the hot hydrothermal fluid at the chimney's exit with a temperature of up to 350°C, which peaks in the infrared but part of its spectrum extends into the visible light.
claims.source: One prominent hypothesis refers to the thermal black body radiation emitted by the hot hydrothermal fluid at the chimney's exit with a temperature of up to 350°C, which peaks in the infrared but part of its spectrum extends into the visible light (Pelli and Chamberlin, 1989; Van Dover et al., 1996; Van Dover et al., 1988; Van Dover and Fry, 1994).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The ability to localize thermal black body radiation could serve both to attract the shrimp to optimal areas for supplying its symbionts with vital, reduced compounds of the hydrothermal fluid, and to allow avoidance of scorching fluid.
claims.source: The ability to localize this radiation could serve both to attract the shrimp to optimal areas for supplying its symbionts with vital, reduced compounds of the hydrothermal fluid, and to allow avoidance of scorching fluid (Van Dover et al., 1989).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Visual cues other than thermal radiation are likely to be also exploited by R. exoculata, related to turbulence, mixing and precipitation, such as chemi-, crystallo-, tribo- and sono-luminescence, for which the emission spectra lie between 450–800 nm.
claims.source: Visual cues other than thermal radiation are likely to be also exploited by R. exoculata, related to turbulence, mixing and precipitation, such as chemi-, crystallo-, tribo- and sono-luminescence, for which the emission spectra lie between 450–800 nm (Reynolds and Lutz, 2001; Tapley et al., 1999; Van Dover et al., 1996; Van Dover and Fry, 1994; White, 2000; White et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Two modes of chemoreception, linked to distinct chemosensory pathways, are distinguished in malacostracan crustaceans: olfaction and distributed chemoreception.
claims.source: Two modes of chemoreception, linked to distinct chemosensory pathways, are distinguished in malacostracan crustaceans (Derby and Weissburg, 2014b; Schmidt and Mellon, 2010): olfaction, which is mediated by the aesthetasc sensilla located on the lateral flagellum of the antenna 1, and distributed chemoreception, which is mediated by the bimodal chemo- and mechanosensory sensilla located mainly on all antennal appendages, the mouthparts, and the walking appendages (Garm et al., 2005; Garm et al., 2003; Garm and Watling, 2013; Mellon, 2014; Mellon, 2012; Schmidt and Gnatzy, 1984).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: R. exoculata presents aesthetascs in similar number and dimensions to other caridean representatives.
claims.source: R. exoculata presents aesthetascs in similar number and dimensions to other caridean representatives (Table 1)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated based on comparative data in Table 1.

claims.claim: R. exoculata presents several bimodal sensilla with different morphologies on the antennal appendages.
claims.source: R. exoculata presents aesthetascs in similar number and dimensions to other caridean representatives (Table 1), as well as several bimodal sensilla with different morphologies on the antennal appendages (Zbinden et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The afferent olfactory input from the olfactory sensory neurons innervating the aesthetascs targets the conspicuous olfactory neuropils, which are lobe-shaped and bilaterally arranged in the deutocerebrum.
claims.source: The afferent olfactory input from the olfactory sensory neurons innervating the aesthetascs targets the conspicuous olfactory neuropils, which are lobe-shaped and bilaterally arranged in the deutocerebrum (Figure 8A–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to figures showing data.

claims.claim: The olfactory neuropils are composed of spherical or cone-shaped dense synaptic neuropils, namely the olfactory glomeruli, which are radially arranged around the periphery of a core of non-synaptic fibers.
claims.source: They are composed of spherical or cone-shaped dense synaptic neuropils, namely the olfactory glomeruli, which are radially arranged around the periphery of a core of non-synaptic fibers.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The olfactory glomeruli are subdivided into a cap, subcap and base regions in several decapod taxa.
claims.source: The olfactory glomeruli are subdivided into a cap, subcap and base regions in several decapod taxa (e.g. Harzsch and Krieger, 2018; Schachtner et al., 2005; Schmidt and Ache, 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The glomeruli of R. exoculata appear to conform to the design principle of subdivision into cap, subcap and base regions, with an identical subdivision.
claims.source: The glomeruli of R. exoculata appear to conform to this design principle, with an identical subdivision (Figure 8E').
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and refers to Figure 8E' showing data.

claims.claim: The dimensions and structural complexity of the olfactory neuropils in R. exoculata do not suggest, judging from comparative brain anatomy, that the loss of the eye's capacity to form images is compensated by sophisticated olfactory abilities.
claims.source: Hence, the dimensions and structural complexity of the olfactory neuropils in R. exoculata do not suggest, judging from comparative brain anatomy, that the loss of the eye's capacity to form images is compensated by sophisticated olfactory abilities.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as an inference from comparative data.

claims.claim: Efficient olfactory abilities would have been especially relevant to probe the chemical environment of R. exoculata, which is dynamic, with strong concentration variations of hydrothermal fluid chemicals as the hydrothermal fluid dilutes with the surrounding seawater.
claims.source: Efficient olfactory abilities would have been especially relevant to probe the chemical environment of R. exoculata, which is dynamic, with strong concentration variations of hydrothermal fluid chemicals as the hydrothermal fluid dilutes with the surrounding seawater.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation.

claims.claim: Sulfide and other chemicals could serve as highly important environmental cues for R. exoculata to locate active edifices as optimal areas to supply its chemoautotrophic symbionts with reduced compounds.
claims.source: Sulfide and other chemicals could serve as highly important environmental cues for R. exoculata (Renninger et al., 1995; Machon et al., 2018) to locate active edifices as optimal areas to supply its chemoautotrophic symbionts with reduced compounds.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sulfide detection is likely mediated by distributed chemoreception, or both distributed chemoreception and olfaction, rather than exclusively olfaction, as it can be detected by the flagella of the antenna two which does not bear aesthetascs.
claims.source: However, sulfide detection is likely mediated by distributed chemoreception, or both distributed chemoreception and olfaction, rather than exclusively olfaction, as it can be detected by the flagella of the antenna two which does not bear aesthetascs (Machon et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Olfaction is involved in the recognition of conspecifics.
claims.source: Olfaction is also involved in the recognition of conspecifics (Breithaupt and Thiel, 2011) and the localization of sexual partners (Wyatt, 2014)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Olfaction is involved in the localization of sexual partners.
claims.source: Olfaction is also involved in the recognition of conspecifics (Breithaupt and Thiel, 2011) and the localization of sexual partners (Wyatt, 2014)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: There is to date no detailed information on the inter-individual interactions in and out of the swarms of R. exoculata.
claims.source: Olfaction is also involved in the recognition of conspecifics (Breithaupt and Thiel, 2011) and the localization of sexual partners (Wyatt, 2014), but there is to date no detailed information on the inter-individual interactions in and out of the swarms of R. exoculata.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: The detection of chemical cues produced by bacteria could appear especially relevant since the sensory antennal appendages of vent shrimp are often covered by a dense bacterial layer, whose roles are currently unknown.
claims.source: The detection of chemical cues produced by bacteria could also appear especially relevant since the sensory antennal appendages of vent shrimp are often covered by a dense bacterial layer, whose roles are currently unknown (Zbinden et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as speculation and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Malacostracan crustaceans display a rich repertoire of complex behavioral patterns related to finding food, shelter and mating partners, kin recognition and brood care, as well as orientation and homing.
claims.source: Malacostracan crustaceans display a rich repertoire of complex behavioral patterns related to finding food, shelter and mating partners, kin recognition and brood care, as well as orientation and homing.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Decapod crustaceans are known for complex social interactions such as communal defensive tactics, the occupation of common shelters, cooperative behavior during long-distance, offshore seasonal migration and the establishment of dominance hierarchies.
claims.source: Decapod crustaceans are also known for complex social interactions such as communal defensive tactics, the occupation of common shelters, cooperative behavior during long-distance, offshore seasonal migration and the establishment of dominance hierarchies (Breithaupt and Thiel, 2011; Derby and Thiel, 2014a; Duffy and Thiel, 2007; Thiel and Watling, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Complex behaviors in crustaceans most likely involve elements of learning and memory.
claims.source: Because such complex behaviors most likely involve elements of learning and memory, higher integrative brain centers are suggested to provide the neuronal substrate for more sophisticated processing underlying such behaviors (review in Sandeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Higher integrative brain centers are suggested to provide the neuronal substrate for more sophisticated processing underlying complex behaviors.
claims.source: Because such complex behaviors most likely involve elements of learning and memory, higher integrative brain centers are suggested to provide the neuronal substrate for more sophisticated processing underlying such behaviors (review in Sandeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Higher integrative centers receive input exclusively from second or higher order neurons but not from any primary sensory afferents.
claims.source: Such centers receive input exclusively from second or higher order neurons but not from any primary sensory afferents (i.e. from the peripheral nervous system) and contain interneurons responding to the stimulation of several different sensory systems.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Higher integrative centers contain interneurons responding to the stimulation of several different sensory systems.
claims.source: Such centers receive input exclusively from second or higher order neurons but not from any primary sensory afferents (i.e. from the peripheral nervous system) and contain interneurons responding to the stimulation of several different sensory systems.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: In the malacostracan brain, the terminal medulla, hemiellipsoid body, and accessory lobe seem to function as higher integrative centers.
claims.source: In the malacostracan brain, the (bilaterally paired) terminal medulla, hemiellipsoid body, and accessory lobe seem to function as higher integrative centers, all three distinct neuropil areas which display a high level of complexity and are notable for their substantial volume (Sandeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla and the closely associated hemiellipsoid body are targeted by axons of the olfactory projection neurons as output pathway of the olfactory neuropil and accessory lobe.
claims.source: The terminal medulla and the closely associated hemiellipsoid body, are targeted by axons of the olfactory projection neurons as output pathway of the olfactory neuropil and accessory lobe (where present; reviews Derby and Weissburg, 2014b; Harzsch and Krieger, 2018; Schmidt, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Evolutionary and functional considerations have focused on possible roles of the terminal medulla and hemiellipsoid body in higher order olfactory processing.
claims.source: Because of these anatomical relationships, evolutionary (Sullivan and Beltz, 2004; Sullivan and Beltz, 2001) and functional considerations (Harzsch and Krieger, 2018; Sandeman et al., 2014; Strausfeld, 2012) have focused on possible roles of these centers in higher order olfactory processing.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla receives input from the visual neuropils in several malacostracans.
claims.source: In addition to the olfactory projection neuron axons, the terminal medulla also receives input from the visual neuropils in several malacostracans (reviewed in Sandeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A specific type of local interneuron associated to the medulla terminalis and the hemiellipsoid body are the parasol cells.
claims.source: A specific type of local interneuron associated to the medulla terminalis and the hemiellipsoid body are the parasol cells (Mellon and Alones, 1997; McKinzie et al., 2003; Mellon et al., 1992a; Mellon, 2000; Mellon et al., 1992b)
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Parasol cells respond to olfactory, tactile, and visual stimuli, thus highlighting their role as elements in higher order integration.
claims.source: A specific type of local interneuron associated to the medulla terminalis and the hemiellipsoid body are the parasol cells (Mellon and Alones, 1997; McKinzie et al., 2003; Mellon et al., 1992a; Mellon, 2000; Mellon et al., 1992b) which respond to olfactory, tactile, and visual stimuli, thus highlighting their role as elements in higher order integration (Mellon and Alones, 1997; Mellon, 2003; Mellon, 2000; Mellon and Wheeler, 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Recent evidence obtained from a brachyuran crab suggests an involvement of the crustacean hemiellipsoid body/terminal medulla complex in memory processes.
claims.source: Recent evidence obtained from a brachyuran crab suggests an involvement of the crustacean hemiellipsoid body/terminal medulla complex in memory processes (Maza et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Considering anatomical similarities of the crustacean hemiellipsoid body and insect mushroom body, Wolff et al. (2017) suggested an involvement in place memory.
claims.source: Furthermore, considering anatomical similarities of the crustacean hemiellipsoid body and insect mushroom body, Wolff et al. (2017) suggested an involvement in place memory.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: During the evolutionary elaboration of malacostracan brains, substantial modifications occurred related to the relative proportion of types of input and investment in size of the various higher integrative centers.
claims.source: During the evolutionary elaboration of malacostracan brains, substantial modifications occurred related to the relative proportion of types of input and investment in size of the various higher integrative centers (Figure 11; Harzsch and Krieger, 2018; Sandeman et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations and Figure 11.

claims.claim: The terminal medulla has a highly complex and highly variable structure, being composed of several, partly confluent neuropil lobes with heterogeneous appearance containing both coarse and fine fibers.
claims.source: Because the terminal medulla has a highly complex and highly variable structure, being composed of several, partly confluent neuropil lobes with heterogeneous appearance containing both coarse and fine fibers (e.g. Blaustein et al., 1988), its architecture so far has not been studied in a comparative context.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The architecture of the terminal medulla has not been studied in a comparative context.
claims.source: Because the terminal medulla has a highly complex and highly variable structure, being composed of several, partly confluent neuropil lobes with heterogeneous appearance containing both coarse and fine fibers (e.g. Blaustein et al., 1988), its architecture so far has not been studied in a comparative context.
claims.evidence: The claim is directly stated.

claims.claim: In its simplest form, the hemiellipsoid body consists of a volume of fine neuropil with little texture that is closely associated with the terminal medulla.
claims.source: In its simplest form, the hemiellipsoid body consists of a volume of fine neuropil with little texture that is closely associated with the terminal medulla (Figures 11A,B,C,F and 12).
